displayQuote: The universe is change; our life is what our thoughts make it

meta.title: Who really said "The universe is change; our life is what our thoughts make it"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: The passage is genuinely Marcus Aurelius — Meditations IV.3 — but this English wording matches no translation we could identify.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The universe is change; our life is what our thoughts make it'?
meta.ogDescription: Meditations IV.3 is real. This English sentence is a translator’s, and we could not establish which translator.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: The passage is real and easy to point at: Meditations Book IV, section 3, six Greek words — “ὁ κόσμος ἀλλοίωσις, ὁ βίος ὑπόληψις.” What we could not establish is whose English this is. No translation we were able to read renders it this way.
answer.confidenceText: The passage is his; this English wording is unattributed

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: A second, that all this visible world changes in a moment, and will be no more; and continually bethink thee to the changes of how many things thou hast already been a witness. ‘The Universe—mutation: Life—opinion.’
trail: Wikiquote’s Marcus Aurelius page ↗ places the sentence at Meditations IV.3 and prints the Greek alongside five different English renderings — Long, Rendall, Farquharson, Boulton / David Widger and one credited to “M. H. Morgan”, which is the wording quoted here.
We read George Long’s 1862 translation ↗ directly: at IV.3 it ends “The universe is transformation: life is opinion.” Not this wording.
We read C. R. Haines’ 1916 Loeb translation ↗ directly: it ends “‘The Universe—mutation: Life—opinion.’” Also not this wording.

We could not identify the “M. H. Morgan” translation Wikiquote names. The Internet Archive holds 17 works by the classicist Morris Hicky Morgan ↗ — Vitruvius, Xenophon, Terence, Lysias, Latin grammars — but no Meditations; and the list of “the chief English translations of Marcus Aurelius” printed in the Project Gutenberg Casaubon edition ↗ (Casaubon, Collier, Thomson, Graves, McCormac, Long, Rendall, Jackson) does not include him. That is not proof no such translation exists — only that we could not find it.
source.excerptNote: That is C. R. Haines’ 1916 Loeb rendering of the closing words — one of several very different English versions of the same six Greek words. George Long’s 1862 translation gives “The universe is transformation: life is opinion.”
source.rightsNote: The Greek original has been in the public domain for centuries, but rights in a quotation attach to the English translation shown. Because we could not identify which translation produced this wording, we cannot date it, and therefore assert no rights status here. Long (1862) and Haines (1916) are both public domain — but neither is the sentence on this page.

author.name: Marcus Aurelius
author.heading: About Marcus Aurelius
author.bio: Marcus Aurelius Antoninus ruled Rome from 161 to 180 AD and wrote the private notebooks we call the Meditations in Greek, mostly on campaign, with no intention of publishing them. Because the text is Greek and the readership is English, almost every famous “Marcus Aurelius quote” is really a translator’s sentence — which is why two people can quote the same passage and share not one word.

misattribution.heading: About this wording
misattribution.intro: Nobody is falsely credited here — Marcus Aurelius wrote the passage. The uncertainty is about whose English is being quoted, which matters more than it sounds: for a Greek author, the sentence people memorise is always a translator’s.

items.why: The second half, “our life is what our thoughts make it”, is an interpretive expansion of two Greek words, ὁ βίος ὑπόληψις — literally “life, judgement”. Both Long (1862) ↗ and Haines (1916) ↗ render it as the single word “opinion”.
Wikiquote ↗ attaches this rendering to “Translation M.H. Morgan”. We were unable to confirm that Morris Hicky Morgan (1859–1910) ever translated the Meditations.

misattribution.truthLine: The safe statement: Marcus Aurelius wrote this thought at Meditations IV.3 ↗; the English sentence you are reading belongs to a translator we could not name.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Book IV, section 3 is the famous passage about retreating into yourself — Marcus telling himself that people go looking for houses in the country and stretches of coast when the only retreat that works is inward. These six words are its closing snap, the compressed reason the retreat works at all.

Everything outside you is in flux and will not hold still long enough to be worth your distress; everything inside you is a judgement you are making, and judgements can be revised. That is the whole Stoic move in one line — which is exactly why translators keep reaching for a longer, warmer English sentence than the Greek actually gives them.
context.pull: Six Greek words. Five English versions, none of them agreeing.
